title: Benchmarking Boltz-2 for relative kinase-inhibitor interaction patterns across conformational states and resistance mutations
abstract: Generative structure-prediction models can directly predict protein-ligand complexes from sequence and ligand information, but their ability to capture pharmacologically relevant kinase-inhibitor interactions remains incompletely understood. We systematically evaluated Boltz-2 using curated biochemical IC50 measurements across eight human kinases, nine clinically used inhibitors, and representative resistance mutations. Although predicted log10(IC50) values showed a compressed dynamic range relative to experimental measurements, mutation-dependent shifts in inhibitor sensitivity, inhibitor selectivity patterns, and overall potency rankings showed substantial agreement with the experimental patterns within the present benchmark. Predicted binding probability showed good discrimination between binder and non-binder pairs within the present benchmark and a consistent inverse relationship with experimental potency. Structural analyses showed that ligand-pose variability was associated with prediction behavior within the evaluated kinase-inhibitor systems, even when kinase-domain structures showed close agreement with the corresponding experimental structures. Larger ligand RMSD values were not associated with larger prediction errors in magnitude, but were linked to systematic shifts in prediction bias, indicating that ligand-pose accuracy and predictive utility are not equivalent measures of Boltz-2 performance. These findings suggest that, within the present benchmark, relative kinase-inhibitor interaction patterns were reproduced more consistently than absolute potency values. We provide a framework for interpreting Boltz-2 outputs within the kinase-inhibitor systems examined here.

title: Three-dimensional mechanical cooperativity optimises epithelial wound healing
abstract: Abstract Epithelial tissues serve as critical physical barriers that protect organs, making their efficient repair essential upon damage. To achieve this, tissues must quickly react, forcing cells to rearrange and accommodate to achieve rapid wound closure. In the Drosophila wing disc, we previously showed how tissue fluidisation accelerated wound healing in 2D. However, the 3D aspect of tissue repair remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover a new mechanism that facilitates tissue repair through changing cell height. We find actomyosin contractile cables at the wound edge connecting the apical and basal cell surfaces, which indent the apical side of the tissue and deform the basement membrane, respectively. To assess the role of the different repair mechanisms, we develop a 3D vertex model allowing independent apical, lateral and basal behaviours. The model predicts that lateral cables play a role in regulating planar cell-cell intercalations, confirmed by Drosophila mutations affecting cell deformations. Our results demonstrate that lateral cables cooperate with the apical purse string to drive 3D cell shape changes and planar cell-cell intercalations for efficient wound repair.

title: A multiphysics computational framework for evaluating ATP response and thermal loading during skeletal muscle photobiomodulation
abstract: Photobiomodulation outcomes depend on how light delivery, tissue heating, and cellular energy-related activity change together. This study develops a three-dimensional computational framework that combines light transport, heat transfer, and a phenomenological model of adenosine triphosphate-related activity in layered skin, fat, and skeletal muscle. The model compares wavelengths of 810, 850, and 900 nm and evaluates the effects of optical power, beam radius, and a 180 s exposure period. Under the common optical condition, 900 nm produces the highest average and maximum light levels in muscle, whereas 850 nm provides an intermediate response and is retained as a representative wavelength for the coupled analyses. Increasing the beam radius markedly reduces local light concentration near the tissue surface while producing little change in the average light level within muscle. At 850 nm with a Gaussian $$1/e^2$$ beam radius of $$w=4$$ mm, the modeled muscle-averaged ATP-related response increases at low optical power, reaches a near-flat maximum of approximately 14.73% between 0.50 and 0.75 W, and then gradually decreases to approximately 12.29% at 2.50 W. In contrast, maximum tissue temperature and cumulative thermal exposure increase continuously with optical power. At 0.75 W, the maximum temperature is 38.584 $$^\circ \textrm{C}$$, while at 2.50 W it rises to 45.857 $$^\circ \textrm{C}$$. A local sensitivity analysis further shows that the magnitude and location of the modeled response maximum depend on the selected inhibition threshold. The results show that greater light delivery does not necessarily produce a greater modeled cellular energy response and may instead increase thermal loading. The framework supports comparison of coupled optical, thermal, and biological trends, but its predictions remain conditional on the selected tissue properties, geometry, and phenomenological parameters. Experimental measurements and higher-fidelity light-transport models are required before quantitative physiological or clinical interpretation.

title: Dynamics of bicoid mRNA localisation and translation dictate morphogen gradient formation
abstract: Abstract The transcription factor Bicoid (Bcd) protein guides early Drosophila patterning and is the best-characterised morphogen. The source of the morphogen, bcd mRNA, is maternally deposited during oogenesis and localised to the anterior pole. When and where Bcd protein is produced and how this protein gradient is dynamically shaped remains contentious. Here, we use the SunTag reporter system to quantitatively examine the spatiotemporal profile of bcd mRNA translation in vivo. We show that association with Processing bodies (P bodies) in mature oocytes prevent premature bcd mRNA translation. Following egg activation, bcd mRNA dissociates from P bodies and translation is observed at the anterior pole. Translation remains largely restricted to the anterior domain throughout early development. At cellularisation, translation ceases and the remaining bcd mRNA associates with reformed P bodies, which appear to block any further translation. We use these observations to create a new modified synthesis-diffusion-degradation model of Bcd gradient, which is consistent with experimental measurements. Overall, our study reveals that bcd mRNA translation is tightly controlled in space and time during oogenesis and early embryogenesis.

abstract: Schwann cells are vital to development and maintenance of the peripheral nervous system, and their dysfunction has been implicated in a range of neurological and neoplastic disorders, including NF2-related schwannomatosis (NF2-SWN). We have developed a human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) model for the study of Schwann-like cell differentiation in health and disease. We performed sequence-based transcriptomics, immunofluorescence-based morphological analysis, and CRISPR-Cas9-based validation of differentiation from hiPSCs derived Schwann cell precursors (SCPs) to terminally differentiated Schwann-like cells (SLCs) representing 6 distinct stages of development across a period of 31 days. To further validate our findings, we performed integrated, cross-species analyses at bulk and single cell resolution. Our hiPSCs model of Schwann cell development shared overlapping gene expression signatures with human amniotic mesenchymal stem cell (hAMSCs) derived SLCs and in vivo mouse models but also revealed unique features that may reflect species-specific aspects of Schwann cell biology. Moreover, we have identified gene co-expression modules that are dynamically regulated during hiPSCs to SLCs differentiation associated with ear and neural development, cell fate determination, the NF2 gene, and extracellular matrix (ECM) organization. Through integrated analysis of multiple datasets and genetic disruption of NF2 via CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing in hiPSC derived SCPs, we have identified transcriptomic signatures suggesting a series of novel ECM associated genes potentially regulated by Merlin, providing a hypothesis-generating framework for future functional studies. The hiPSC model generated in this study further provides a system for studying NF2-regulated gene expression throughout Schwann-like cell development in the context of widely available data on iPSC Schwann cells and rare diseases that lack effective treatments such as NF2-SWN.

title: Reversion to the Meta Body Form of Life after Complete Cell Death in Pure Liquid Water
abstract: The prevailing view holds that simpler animate beings predating the dawn of cellular life once existed, yet they have long since vanished from the present-day Earth. Our hypothesis posits that these animate beings persist to this day. To this end, we devised a long-term experiment spanning over a decade, keeping Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) within a sealed aqueous system of pure water. The findings illustrated that, upon the complete cell death (CCD) of the S. aureus, as cellular remnants progressively succumbed to dissolution, the aqueous solution underwent self-purification, bringing forth a class of lipid bilayer membrane microspheres containing RNA and proteins. These structures maintained long-term sustainable stability within the thermodynamic storm of water molecules and underwent dynamic size fluctuations over time - collectively exhibited phenomena indicative of being "alive". This study reveals that the cell, upon complete cell death, undergoes reversion to a living entity simpler than the cell itself - the Meta Body (MB). The discovery of MB opens an entire re-conceptualization of what death ultimately brings.

title: Buried Ion-Pairs Reshape Folding Pathways of Artificial Proteins
abstract: Ion-pairs are central charged motifs that control the biological function of several proteins. Yet, the physical principles linked to the formation of ion-pairs during protein folding remain poorly understood. Here, we show that buried ion-pairs of de novo-designed helical bundle proteins reshape the folding pathways by introducing kinetic barriers that are overcome by a hydrophobic collapse linked to packing of the protein core. By combining protein design with co-translational folding studies, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that introduction of a buried ion-pair leads to a shifted folding transition that balances desolvation and electrostatic interactions within the protein and the bulk solvent. Moreover, we find that the folding pathway is sensitive to modifications in non-polar interactions and motifs that electrostatically shield the ion-pair from its surroundings. Our combined findings provide a blueprint for understanding how functional motifs affect protein folding and how mutation of charged networks alter the stability of proteins.

abstract: Production of glycoconjugate vaccines has long relied upon chemical methods which are highly complex and expensive, resulting in vaccines that are not widely affordable. Heterologous bioconjugation methods, such as Protein-Glycan Coupling Technology (PGCT), have emerged as a path to significantly cheaper manufacture using safe host organisms, such as Escherichia coli, for recombinant glycoconjugate expression. PGCT glycoconjugate synthesis components are typically encoded across three plasmids and require the addition of exogenous chemical inducers for gene expression. In this study, we utilise modular DNA assembly to generate a single constitutive plasmid for biosynthesis of a Streptococcus pyogenes rhamnose polysaccharide glycoconjugate vaccine. This approach resulted in a greater than seven-fold glycoconjugate yield as well as simplified cell culture conditions compared to the traditional three plasmid inducible system. Importantly, given the modular nature of this method, this innovation could be applied to the manufacture of glycoconjugate vaccines against a range of pathogens.

title: Potential energy release rate for solids with bounded domains during evolutions involving changes to boundaries and boundary data
abstract: We investigate the rate of change of equilibrium potential energy for nonlinear elastic solids undergoing evolutions that may involve changes in body geometry, material properties, applied tractions, and prescribed displacements. We represent such an evolution by a one-parameter family of variational problems and identify a class of these families for which the potential-energy release rate is well defined. Particular attention is given to the formulation of the potential energy at each evolution state: each constituent variational problem must yield the appropriate equilibrium state, while its equilibrium value must also correctly represent the physical change in potential energy between states. Within this framework, we derive a closed-form expression for the potential-energy release rate for solids with bounded domains, allowing for spatially nonuniform material evolution, sharp material interfaces, and evolving boundary geometry and prescribed boundary data. The expression is determined entirely by the equilibrium solution at the state under consideration and by the quantities prescribing the local evolution, so neighboring equilibrium problems need not be solved. Finally, we apply the result to the extension of a notch in a two-dimensional elastic body and show that the resulting potential-energy release rate reduces to the classical $J$-integral.

title: Arrested phase separation and amorphous patterns in charged binary fluids
abstract: Frustration generated by competing interactions can stabilise patterns with tunable lengthscales which evade indefinite coarsening and macroscopic phase separation. Here we investigate a charged binary fluid in which the tendency toward phase separation is opposed by screened electrostatic repulsion. Combining analytics and numerical simulations, we identify a regime of arrested phase separation characterised by finite-wavelength instability. The resulting states include droplet and labyrinthine phases in two dimensions, and droplets, concentric shells and tubular structures in three dimensions. Surprisingly, some of these structures are amorphous morphologies that emerge reproducibly from different initial conditions. Free-energy estimates suggest that these disordered structures may be thermodynamically stabilised by frustration, rather than being kinetically trapped. Our results identify a simple mechanism through which the competition between phase separation and screened electrostatics can generate equilibrium amorphous microphases with glassy features.

title: Shear-driven arrest of dip-coating film entrainment
abstract: A plate withdrawn from a bath of partially wetting liquid entrains a film above a critical velocity. Here, we show that this critical threshold can be substantially increased by the presence of a laminar gas flow opposed to the plate velocity that exerts a tangential shear stress on the liquid-gas interface. Using two-phase immiscible Navier-Stokes simulations and confining the gas to a narrow channel, we derive a closed-form expression for the interfacial stress, which combined with lubrication theory relates the thickness of the film and the contact line velocity to the applied shear stress. As the gas velocity is increased, the film thins and the contact line velocity slows down, until the imposed shear overcomes the drag of the moving plate and entrainment is arrested. As in the quiescent case, the velocity mismatch between plate and contact line is independent of the plate velocity and is set by the applied shear alone. We find that one set of varying gas flow simulations, with constant critical plate velocity, therefore determines the critical gas flow for every smaller plate velocity.

abstract: by Jhon A. Zabaleta-Santisteban, Angel J. Medina-Medina, Katerin M. Tuesta-Trauco, Abner S. Rivera-Fernandez, Teodoro B. Silva-Melendez, Marlen A. Grandez-Alberca, Julio Puscan-Rojas, Rolando Salas López, Manuel Oliva-Cruz, Alexander Cotrina-Sanchez, Nilton B. Rojas-Briceño, Jhonsy O. Silva-López, Darwin Gómez-Fernández, Santos Triunfo Leiva-Espinoza, Angel F. Huaman-Pilco, Elgar Barboza Identifying climatically suitable areas for cacao cultivation (Theobroma cacao L.) is essential to guide sustainable intensification, territorial planning, and compliance with emerging environmental standards in tropical regions. This study assessed the current climatic suitability of cacao in the Amazonas department (northwestern Peru) using an ensemble modeling approach implemented in biomod2, integrating bioclimatic, topographic, and edaphic predictors with spatial biophysical exclusion criteria, legal conservation constraints, regulatory eligibility associated with the European Union Deforestation-Free Products Regulation (EUDR), and local phytosanitary evidence. A total of 403 quality-controlled presence records were used to calibrate multiple machine-learning algorithms under cross-validation, retaining only those with high predictive performance (AUC > 0.9; TSS > 0.7). Decision tree–based models, particularly Random Forest and XGBoost, showed the best individual performance, while the consensus model exhibited greater spatial stability and overall accuracy. Results indicate that approximately 14.8% of the regional territory presents high climatic suitability under current conditions, concentrated in inter-Andean valleys and low- to mid-elevation zones, with thermal seasonality identified as the main environmental predictor. However, the incorporation of territorial and regulatory constraints substantially reduced the effectively available area, especially under the EUDR scenario, demonstrating that cacao expansion potential is strongly conditioned by conservation and regulatory frameworks. High-priority degraded areas emerged as focal opportunities for productive restoration through agroforestry systems. Phytosanitary validation (2021–2024) revealed high spatial concordance between areas of greatest climatic suitability and the prevalence and incidence of major cacao pathogens and pests, particularly Moniliophthora roreri and M. perniciosa, confirming that optimal climatic niches for cultivation also favor biotic pressure. Overall, this study provides an integrative framework combining climatic modeling, territorial management, and phytosanitary risk, delivering robust scientific inputs to inform public policy, land-use planning, and sustainable cacao production strategies in the Amazon.

title: How Fluctuations Control Chiral Symmetry Breaking in Reacting Mixtures of Chiral Molecules
abstract: The pronounced chiral asymmetry of biomolecules is a defining feature of living systems, yet the mechanisms by which such asymmetry emerged remain unresolved. Chiral symmetry breaking may have occurred under prebiotic conditions in systems with sufficiently small molecular populations for intrinsic fluctuations to play an important role. Here, we investigate how finite-population fluctuations affect chiral-state selection, the characteristic time for symmetry breaking, and stochastic switching between chiral states in a system driven by autocatalysis and mutual antagonism. We determine how these dynamical processes scale with particle number and derive an analytical expression for the probability of selecting either chiral state as a function of the initial enantiomeric bias. We further calculate the mean selection time for different initial biases and show that, for weak mutual antagonism, fluctuations can induce transitions between opposite chiral states. These results characterize how finite-population fluctuations control both the emergence and stability of molecular chirality in autocatalytic chemical systems.

abstract: The effect of mechanical stresses and deformations upon the behavior and properties of cells and tissues is a topic of paramount interest in the field of biophysics. For boosting the understanding in this field, it is important to develop devices for the application of simple deformations in order to probe the cellular response to the basic mechanical transformations. While a number of stretching devices have been developed, in-plane shearing deformation has been little investigated. Here, a new device is introduced that allows the application of homogeneous in-plane shear upon a cell monolayer while imaging the sample with a commercial optical microscope. A description of the faced experimental challenges is reported and a full characterization is presented. It is demonstrated the capability of the device to apply reproducible, controlled and homogeneous shear of both single cells and confluent cellular monolayers.

title: Imbibition dynamics under dissolution-driven fluid thickening
abstract: The imbibition of milk into a biscuit provides an example of a broader class of processes in which a liquid invades a porous material, dissolving components of the solid and thereby modifying its own rheology. This coupling between imbibition, dissolution, and evolving fluid rheology also occurs in food processing, filtration, and reactive porous media. While the resulting changes in fluid viscosity are known to affect imbibition, a quantitative description of how this evolving rheology determines the imbibition dynamics is still lacking. Here, we establish such a description for dissolution-driven fluid thickening. For a capillary tube in the well-mixed limit, we derive a generalized Washburn law showing that the evolving viscosity can be incorporated through a rescaled time given by the accumulated inverse viscosity. This predicts a collapse of the imbibition dynamics for different dissolution rates, which we confirm numerically using coupled free-surface and solute-transport simulations. When diffusion is slower, concentration and viscosity become spatially heterogeneous, resulting in a weaker retardation of the advancing liquid than predicted by the well-mixed theory. We then consider disordered porous media and quantify how dissolution-driven thickening and variations in pore geometry affect the dynamics. Our results extend the classical Washburn description to imbibition with evolving fluid properties and provide a quantitative basis for understanding fluid uptake when interactions with the solid progressively modify the rheology of the invading liquid.

abstract: Spatially-resolved mass spectrometry could contribute to the understanding of biological processes. Atom probe tomography (APT) is a technique which could, in principle, fill an analytical gap for nanoscale mass spectrometry. Yet, because of a limited understanding of the process of fragmentation of biomolecules, biological or biochemical interpretation of the obtained data has so far not been successful. Here, we report on analyses of synthetic and biogenic pigmented calcite minerals. The purple coloration of Sphaerechinus granularis sea urchin spines is due to the occlusion of polyhydroxylated naphthoquinone (PHNQ) molecules, mainly spinochrome A, within the calcite phase. Peaks relating to these pigments as well as to other intra-crystalline macromolecules were identified by APT analysis of the purple spine region with comparison to measurements of synthetic calcite single crystals, calcite crystals doped with PHNQ, and the uncoloured (white) region of sea urchin spines. To facilitate the molecular identification of peaks appearing solely in purple-coloured spines, which are possible fragments from PHNQ, we introduce novel APT data filtering techniques based on spatial and temporal correlations in the detection of ions of targeted mass-to-charge state ratios. This allows us to discuss the fragmentation of organic molecules under field conditions and improve the identification of peaks in the mass spectrum, while also determining nanoscale spatial distribution of fragments related to specifically targeted biomolecules in 3D and elucidate the relationship these organic pigment molecules have to the calcite lattice and inorganic elements such as magnesium. The study aims to improve identification of complex molecular structures by APT, including organic molecules, with the potential ability to provide structural information at a near-atomic scale for a range of materials.

abstract: Low affinity chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) can clinically outperform high-affinity variants, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying affinity-dependent activity remain unclear. At low CAR expression on dense CD19 bilayers, low-affinity CAT CARs formed more mature and dynamic synapses, recruited ZAP70 more efficiently, and showed faster microcluster motion. Our data support a model in which weaker, lower-affinity CAR-antigen interactions promote receptor turnover, microcluster mobility, and signaling-adaptor recruitment, thereby enhancing downstream signal propagation. Our work provides a mechanistic basis for the superior functional performance reported for affinity-tuned CD19 CAR-T cells.

title: A Geometrical Class of Population Growth Models, across Scales and Population Structures
abstract: We develop a general geometrical framework for growth processes in which the growth rate depends exponentially on the number of active growth-supporting components. The framework separates the fraction of active components from the size of the accessible component space, allowing qualitatively different growth laws to arise from the same underlying construction. Bacterial population growth provides an example of a fixed-size component space controlled primarily by activation and deactivation, whereas examples such as human population growth or speciation provide an expanding component space in which interactions between individuals promote further growth. This motivates a Replicative geometrical law, dX/dt= X exp({beta} X^{gamma}), whose exponent characterizes the scaling of the effective growth-supporting component space and is tested against historical human-population regimes and eukaryotic lineage-through-time data. For innovation indicators such as patents and arXiv manuscript submissions, where an existing item need not itself reproduce, the same construction motivates a Direct Geometrical production law without the prefactor X. The framework therefore provides a common description of fixed and expanding component spaces while distinguishing Replicative from Direct Geometrical growth.

title: Boundary-contact repolarization provides a mechanism for directional guidance of neural crest cell collectives
abstract: Neural crest cells (NCCs) provide a well-established system for investigating collective migration during embryonic development and exhibit migratory behaviors with parallels to cancer invasion. Previous studies establish roles for co-attraction, contact inhibition of locomotion, polarity persistence, and tissue confinement in guiding NCC migration. However, it remains unclear whether NCC migration in confined environments occurs through spatial restriction alone or also through a repolarization response induced by contact with boundaries of confinement. By developing a computational model that couples self-generated chemical transport with contact-mediated repolarization and mechanical interactions, we show that cell-boundary contact can reorient cell polarity and sustain directional migration under confinement, whereas no persistent collective direction emerges without confinement. Moreover, suppressing contact-mediated repolarization from non-permissive confinement boundaries while preserving the mechanical interactions prevents sustained directional migration, suggesting that spatial restriction alone is insufficient in the model. Together, these findings establish an experimentally testable mechanism through which self-generated chemical signals and contact with confining tissues jointly regulate collective guidance of NCCs. These insights provide a basis for investigating developmental migration defects and potential strategies to regulate collective tissue invasion.

abstract: Most systems trained by equilibrium propagation or coupled learning are in the same class as multi-layer perceptrons: while they may be universal function approximators, they struggle to learn associative tasks which are easy for transformers. Equilibrium propagation relies on a bidirectional flow of information through the physical system between input and output. The reverse flow is broken by more complex nonlinear systems, such as those performing multiplication which is needed to express dot-product attention. Here we explicitly restore this bidirectional flow by introducing extra circuit elements for this purpose into a double or dyadic circuit. We then use these ideas to construct an attention mechanism exploiting the exponential current law of sub-threshold MOSFET devices. We show that in simulations this circuit can be trained to perform a simple in-context learning task, despite using realistic reverse components which transmit only an approximate gradient. For this training to succeed we need cross-entropy loss (not mean squared error). We generate nudges appropriate for this loss using a novel floating circuit element, based on the same MOSFET sub-circuit used for softmax. We train the resistors in this circuit using the Lion optimiser, which can be implemented using one capacitor per parameter to store local memory of past gradient estimates.

title: Ecology of AI Agents: Collaboration Creates a Population Threshold for Takeoff
abstract: AI agents can now conduct real-world cyberattacks, scale up capabilities with the number of agents, and collectively pursue misaligned goals to obtain rewards. Together, these factors raise the risk of a population explosion of misaligned agents: agents could compromise computers and secretly deploy additional agents, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where larger populations develop greater collective cyber capability and expand further. This raises a fundamental question: What determines whether a population of misaligned agents remains contained or takes off into this self-reinforcing cycle? This population-level problem is ecological safety: unlike individual-agent or multi-agent safety with a fixed population, it concerns the dynamics of the population itself. Here, we develop an ecological theory of AI-agent populations based on a population growth equation in which fitness (growth rate) depends on cybersecurity capability. We show that, without collaboration, the population takes off only when individual-agent capability exceeds a critical threshold. With collaboration, however, collective cybersecurity capability increases with population size. This creates a critical population threshold: below it, the population declines; above it, the population takes off, even though individual-agent capability has not changed. In ecology, this phenomenon is known as the strong Allee effect. Because red teaming a small group of agents cannot guarantee ecological safety in larger populations, our theory calls for ecological red teaming and population pacing: gradually deploying larger agent populations in controlled environments, while measuring how cyber capability scales with population size, and estimating the critical population size for takeoff. Capability gains may lower this threshold, requiring re-estimation for each new model generation.

abstract: The prospect of imaging single biomolecules, viruses and cells with intense, ultrashort X-ray pulses has driven the development of X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs). From 32 788 diffraction patterns of single trimers in random orientations, we reconstructed the 3D electron density to a resolution of 3.8 nm, limited by the detector geometry. These results show that membrane-protein complexes can be imaged in vacuo with X-ray lasers, an important step towards ultrafast diffractive imaging of single macromolecules.

abstract: Thermodynamic cycles are the foundation of energy conversion across natural and engineered systems, transforming heat into useful work. These findings demonstrate that thermodynamic cycles can emerge when autonomous systems navigate their environments, offering an artificial analog of organisms that forage for energy across spatial resources.

abstract: Perturbation screens hold the potential to systematically map regulatory processes at single-cell resolution, yet modeling and predicting transcriptome-wide responses to perturbations remains a major computational challenge. Here, we present the latent causal diffusion (LCD), a generative model that frames single-cell gene expression as a stationary diffusion process observed under measurement noise. LCD outperforms established approaches in predicting the distributional shifts of unseen perturbation combinations in single-cell RNA-sequencing screens while simultaneously learning a mechanistic dynamical system of gene regulation. To interpret these learned dynamics, we develop an approach we call causal linearization via perturbation responses (CLIPR), which yields an approximation of the direct causal effects between all genes modeled by the diffusion. CLIPR provably identifies causal effects under a linear drift assumption and recovers causal structure in both simulated systems and a genome-wide perturbation screen, where it clusters genes into coherent functional modules and resolves causal relationships that standard differential expression analysis cannot. The LCD-CLIPR framework bridges generative modeling with causal inference to predict unseen perturbation effects and map the underlying regulatory mechanisms of the transcriptome.

abstract: How organisms develop in dynamic environmental conditions is a fundamental question. We developed an unbiased dimensional reduction approach, based on Singular Value Decomposition, to reliably identify the dynamic modes of segmentation clock oscillations across all temperature conditions. We reveal that the two major dynamic modes show opposite temperature sensitivities: While the temporal oscillation (mode 1) varies strongly with temperature, the spatial phase gradient (mode 2) appears largely temperature invariant. In addition, we found developmental parameters with intermediate, subscaled temperature responses, such as axis elongation. We used theoretical modeling to understand how dynamic modes emerge from the underlying local oscillation dynamics and axis elongation. We then exposed embryos to circadian and ultradian temperature cycles to reveal dynamic response patterns of oscillations and axis elongation, and found how these responses are integrated into morphological features. Combined, our theoretical–experimental results support a model in which the dynamic integration of temporal (i.e. segmentation clock related) and spatial (i.e. axis elongation) processes, in particular their subscaled temperature response patterns, quantitatively compensate each other to yield a robust, temperature-invariant axis patterning outcome.

Here, we consider an approach grounded in informatics and algorithmic thermodynamics for how neural systems respond to different patterns of information in different ways, with a focus on the relationship between the information entropy of a signal and a new proposed quantity we term information enthalpy, which represents the internal resource of structured information within a system available to be used for predictions and other forms of work. To evaluate the capacity of the external signals to increase information enthalpy in the system, we introduce the information enthalpy potential (IEP) as a defined metric. We propose and implement a method for quantifying the amount of potential information enthalpy - the IEP - in a given signal across a range of example signals. We offer a conjecture of how information enthalpy may be treated by neural systems within a biological framework before showing how it may integrate and offer falsifiability to existing approaches such as the Free Energy Principle. This framework is also positioned in light of the role of neural criticality. Finally, we postulate a testable and falsifiable framework where the distinct mechanisms within each driver interact through a described n-body-inspired model to govern the "motion" of a neural system through a high dimensional state-space. Through these processes, it is proposed that these features form the most fundamental basis of the neural drivers that give rise to the complexity of adaptive behaviors that are commonly called: intelligence.

title: Small-Molecule Inhibitors Allosterically Control Bruton's Tyrosine Kinase Assembly on the Membrane
abstract: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (Btk) is the target of small-molecule, active site inhibitors for treatment of lymphomas and leukemias. Beyond its catalytic activity, Btk participates in signaling assemblies through scaffolding functions that can contribute to drug resistance. Here, we show that Btk forms micron-scale assemblies on membranes and that this behavior is allosterically controlled by ligand binding at the active site. Using supported lipid bilayers and total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy, we find that nucleotides and inhibitors including ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, and dasatinib promote assembly, whereas fenebrutinib and pirtobrutinib prevent assembly. Membrane organization is independent of catalysis but correlates with ligand-dependent changes in Btk conformational flexibility measured by hydrogen-deuterium exchange. These results reveal a previously unrecognized connection between active-site ligand binding and mesoscale membrane organization, demonstrating that kinase inhibitors can control Btk behavior beyond suppression of catalytic activity.

title: Molecular sterics guide tmRNA translocation on the ribosome
abstract: Translation of defective mRNA transcripts can lead to the formation of stalled ``non-stop'' ribosome complexes. To rescue these ribosomes, bacteria have evolved a mechanism called trans-translation that is mediated by transfer-messenger RNA (tmRNA) and small protein B (SmpB). During the translocation step of trans-translation, the stalled mRNA is ejected and the reading frame found in the mRNA-like domain (MLD) of tmRNA is loaded into the mRNA channel. The ribosome then translates the new template, thereby tagging the nascent protein for degradation. While structures of tmRNA-SmpB on the ribosome have been available for years, little is known about the molecular factors that govern the dynamics of tmRNA translocation. Here, we use an energetically smooth model (i.e. SMOG) to simulate translocation of tmRNA-SmpB, which reveals that the structure of the ribosome gives rise to a preferred sequence of conformational substeps. Specifically, the tRNA-like domain (TLD) translocates, then the MLD loads, and finally the C-terminal tail of SmpB rearranges. These steps are interdependent and associated with a range of sterically-induced barriers that regulate the kinetics. This provides a structural and energetic framework for understanding, and ultimately controlling, the dynamics of trans-translation.

title: Structural Basis for Near Infrared Absorption and Noncanonical Photoisomerization in Neorhodopsin
abstract: In retinal proteins, light absorption leads to a double bond isomerization of the chromophore, followed by conformational relaxations that drive functional protein rearrangements. The balance between photoisomerization and radiative or non-radiative decays of the excited state is adjusted to the demands of the respective photoreceptor function. The molecular determinants controlling the excited state processes remain poorly understood and are the focus of this combined crystallographic, spectroscopic, and theoretical work on the recently discovered neorhodopsin (NeoR). NeoR exhibits a highly red-shifted and fluorescent dark state and selectively photoisomerizes from all-trans to 7-cis. We show that the local electrostatic environment reduces the negative charge density near the Schiff base and suppresses torsional motion around the canonical C13=C14 isomerization site of microbial rhodopsins. Instead, the chromophore-binding pocket permits only low-efficiency C7=C8 isomerization, accompanied by polyene inversion, {beta}-ionone ring displacement, and Schiff base deprotonation. Consequently, unlike other retinal photoreceptors, NeoR undergoes structural changes localized near the {beta}-ionone ring.

title: Chain-Length-Dependent Interactions of Polyethylene Nanoplastics with Human Catalase reveals Size based Nanoplastic Toxicity
abstract: Nanoplastic contamination is increasingly recognized as a biochemical stressor, yet the molecular determinants governing how polymer fragment size dictates protein-level interactions remain poorly understood. Here, we combine molecular docking and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize the interaction of polyethylene (PE) oligomers of increasing length (n = 3, 5, 7, and 14 repeat units) with human catalase, a tetrameric heme enzyme central to cellular antioxidant defense. Single-chain simulations reveal that short PE fragments (3-, 5-, and 7-mer) migrate from an initial domain-connector pose toward a heme-proximal, previously characterized inhibitor-binding site, whereas the 14-mer remains kinetically confined to a peripheral surface site, implicating short-chain PE as a potential catalase inhibitor. In multichain corona systems, backbone dynamics show a non-monotonic, chain-length-dependent destabilization, with the 3- and 5-mer inducing the greatest structural perturbation and the 14-mer best preserving native-like dynamics despite forming an extensive, percolating surface network across all four subunits. MM-PBSA free energy decomposition identifies van der Waals interactions as the dominant thermodynamic driver of binding, while electrostatic surface mapping indicates that cationic surface patches instead govern long-range spatial targeting of PE chains. These findings establish a framework linking nanoplastic fragment size to protein-level toxicity, with direct implications for assessing the biochemical risk of environmentally weathered polyethylene.

title: Senescence-induced Spatio-temporal Re-organization of the Nuclear Lamina Dynamic Landscape at Single-molecule Level in Live Human RPE Cells
abstract: A defining hallmark of cellular senescence is the extensive remodeling of the nuclear lamina (NL) in both structure, composition, and its interactions with lamina-associated genomic domains. However, how such senescence-induced changes could quantitatively impact the spatio-temporal dynamics of NL interactions at the single-molecule level remain poorly understood. Herein, using human retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells as model system, we establish a robust, chemically inducible cellular senescence model capable of recapitulating key signatures of the senescence-associated phenotype. Senescent RPE cells exhibit distinct alteration patterns in the expression of various NL components, including lamin B receptor (LBR) and emerin, two key mediators of NL-chromatin interactions. Importantly, live-cell diffusion measurements via imaging FCS reveal globally enhanced mobility for both LBR and emerin, indicative of weakened NL anchoring in senescent cells. Single-molecule tracking and super-resolved STAR mapping further unveil distinct, multi-modal re-organization of their NL-binding dynamics in both space and time (especially in the form of LBR binding "hotspots" where multiple stable binding events cluster to effect more extended and prolonged interaction), in line with their respective expression-level alterations and differential lamin interactions. Moreover, correlative mapping uncovers a strong spatial coupling between reduced LBR mobility and highly condensed constitutive heterochromatin domains at the NL, which become dispersed during senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the re-organization of NL dynamic landscape at single-molecule level as a critical and previously under-explored facet of senescence-induced NL remodeling, and point to a synergistic interplay between physical de-anchoring, dynamic attenuation of stable NL-binding and spatial restructuring of chromatin architecture in modulating NL-heterochromatin contacts to potentially effect global changes in senescence-associated gene expression.

title: Transcription factor interactions promote binding to non-cognate DNA sites
abstract: Recruitment of transcription factors (TFs) to non-cognate DNA sequences is widely observed, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that, within the nucleosome, Sox2 can bind an Oct4 motif, interact with the Oct4 POU-specific domain, and displace the Oct4 homeodomain. We also observe Sox2 binding at multiple near-canonical and non-canonical DNA sites, with these interactions promoted by a second Sox2 molecule or by nearby nucleosome-bound Oct4. The TF-TF interactions can bridge across DNA gyres, bringing together binding sites that are distant in linear DNA but spatially proximal on the nucleosome. We further find that Sox2 can engage across nucleosomal DNA gyres through loop regions and/or intrinsically disordered segments, providing an additional mode of chromatin binding. Together, our structural and biochemical data reveal how TF-TF interactions change DNA recognition on the nucleosome, enabling binding to non-cognate sequences and expanding the repertoire of pioneer factor interactions on chromatin.

title: Quantification of cellular contributions to multi-cellular pattern formation
abstract: Multi-cellular pattern formation is a key process in organism development, regeneration, and disease. Such multi-cellular patterns include, for instance, cell density and gene expression patterns. Here, we develop a cell-track-based method that quantifies how much individual cellular processes contribute to the emergence of large-scale patterns. These cellular processes include changes in cellular expression levels, cell motion, cell divisions, and apoptosis. We validate our method using synthetic data, before demonstrating it on two sets of experimental data. Our method is purely geometric and does not require any mechanistic assumptions about the underlying pattern-forming processes, making it very generic and robust. It thus enables unbiased, data-driven study of the mechanisms driving pattern formation across a broad class of systems.

title: Latent-Space Residue-Pair Networks from Molecular Dynamics Distinguish Ligand-Activated and SAVI-Associated STING
abstract: Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) provides an informative model system for developing methods to extract and compare residue-pair fluctuation patterns from molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories. We combined a one-dimensional convolutional autoencoder trained on apo STING with temporal mean pooling, Mahalanobis-distance clustering, and residue-pair similarity networks to compare apo, ligand-bound, and SAVI-associated multi-mutant datasets using 25-dimensional latent descriptors. Networks constructed from clusters capturing state-dependent fluctuation patterns showed lid-dominated organization in the ligand-bound dataset and a1b1-enriched, structurally distributed relationships involving residue 281 in the multi-mutant dataset. These findings identify contrasting residue-pair fluctuation signatures in the analyzed trajectories and provide an interpretable framework for generating hypotheses about ligand-associated and mutation-associated dynamic allostery.

title: Microscopic collisions govern macroscopic aerotactic spreading through emergent transport coefficients
abstract: Collective migration is often attributed to complex cell-cell communication, yet coordinated multicellular dynamics can also emerge in organisms lacking social interactions. Continuum descriptions successfully capture such behaviors but generally rely on phenomenological transport coefficients whose microscopic origin remains elusive. Here we show that these coefficients emerge from cell-cell collisions and can be independently determined from experiments. We investigate the aerotactic dispersal of confined colonies of the solitary amoeba Acanthamoeba castellanii, in which oxygen consumption continuously reshapes the local environment to generate self-organized guidance cues. Combining quantitative videomicroscopy, oxygen mapping with phosphorescent sensing films, and oxygen-controlled microfluidics, we directly measure both the oxygen landscape and the aerotactic response governing colony expansion. We then develop a Patlak-Keller-Segel (PKS) -type drift-diffusion model whose transport coefficients are entirely determined from independent experiments and microscopic-to-macroscopic modeling approach, without adjustable parameters. The model quantitatively reproduces the observed dynamics, including the coexistence of a fast ballistic front and a trailing transient accumulation band. We show that both diffusion and aerotactic transport are modulated by the same collision-controlled mechanism through density-dependent changes in cell persistence. More generally, our results establish transport coefficients as measurable emergent properties bridging microscopic cell dynamics and macroscopic collective behavior, providing a predictive framework for oxygen-guided migration in living active matter.

title: Adaptive motility and feeding strategies of deep-branching predatory protists
abstract: Heterotrophic flagellates play a major role in nutrient recycling and shaping aquatic microbial communities. Many motile species have evolved diverse predatory strategies to exploit microbial prey, from bacteria to small eukaryotes. Excavates, deep-branching eukaryotic lineages with distinctive biflagellate morphology and conserved cytoskeletal features, exhibit varied feeding behaviours, including grazing, raptorial feeding, and filter-feeding. However, the temporal dynamics of their motility, feeding, and spatial distribution in relation to bacterial population density remain under-explored. Here, we quantify the behavioural ecology of excavates using high-resolution, single-cell tracking and quantitative analysis. Focussing on two Discoba species - the marine Jakoba libera and freshwater Reclinomonas americana - we identify different behavioural patterns: J. libera swims, forages and feeds, while R. americana swims and feeds. Prey availability differentially affects motility: J. libera increases the number of swimming cells when food is scarce, while R. americana shows the opposite trend. Spatial statistics reveal fundamental differences in their feeding and redistribution strategies. J. libera acts as an active forager, whereas R. americana behaves as a strict filter feeder. A third species, the anaerobic Kipferlia bialata (from a different clade), adopts a foraging strategy similar to J. libera. Together, these results elucidate the adaptive relationship between prey availability, feeding modes, and motility in bacteriovorous excavate flagellates, offering new insights into the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of microbial predators.

title: Occupancy-driven attenuation in radiation-sensitive chromatin domains as a statistical-mechanical model of the overkill effect and RBE maximum
abstract: The reduction in biological effectiveness at high linear energy transfer (LET), commonly referred to as the overkill effect, remains an active area of investigation in high-LET radiobiology. Here, we present a statistical-mechanical framework in which attenuation emerges from the progressive occupancy of a finite population of radiation-sensitive chromatin domains. An effective free-energy formalism is used to describe the equilibrium occupancy state, yielding an LET-dependent occupancy fraction and an attenuation function representing the fraction of chromatin domains remaining available for the formation of additional biologically independent lethal events. The model predicts a continuous occupancy transition accompanied by a fluctuation maximum, identifying a characteristic LET range in which occupancy effects become most pronounced. When combined with a previously published LET-dependent damage-production model for carbon-ion irradiation of V79 cells, the framework predicts a maximum in lethal-lesion yield followed by a decline despite continued increases in damage production. The qualitative comparison of the RBE data in published works reveals the typical pattern of growth, peak value, and decline of the biological effectiveness, although the predicted values of the RBE continue to be lower than the experimental ones. These results suggest that finite chromatin-domain occupancy may provide a possible physical interpretation of attenuation, the overkill effect, and the emergence of an RBE maximum.

title: De Novo Design of Flavoproteins with Controlled Excited State Dynamics
abstract: Designing photochemical properties in proteins is a frontier challenge in biomolecular design, which, when realised, will open new avenues in catalysis and biomolecular electronics. Here we demonstrate an integrated computational design framework, supported by ultrafast spectroscopy, combining protein design, quantum mechanical/molecular mechanics molecular dynamics (QM/MM MD) and electronic structure calculations, to control flavin excited states in de novo proteins. Iterative design yields FC-4D2, a flavocytochrome with covalently bound flavin and non-covalently bound heme B and Fl-4D2, where the heme-binding site is removed. Both proteins are highly thermostable, and access all physiologically relevant flavin redox and protonation states, while high-resolution X-ray crystallography confirms the near-[A]ngstrom-level accuracy in design. Incorporating QM/MM MD and linear-response time-dependent density functional theory (LR-TDDFT) into the design workflow enables engineering of a flavin-tryptophan charge-transfer variant, Fl-4D2CT, that modifies the flavin absorption spectrum, substantially alters its redox properties and suppresses fluorescence. Ultrafast studies reveal how protein design reshapes the excited state relaxation timescale and mechanism. Our study establishes a modular strategy for programming flavin photochemistry in designed proteins.

title: Bio-VQVAE: multivariate and multi-scale time-series generation for bioprocess data augmentation
abstract: Biomanufacturing digitalization relies heavily on data-driven modeling, yet the scarcity of high-quality labeled data remains a bottleneck. Multivariate fermentation data exhibit temporal patterns at multiple scales and complex statistical dependencies among process-state and operational variables. Current time-series generation methods often have difficulty preserving multi-scale temporal patterns and statistical dependencies among process variables. This paper proposes Bio-VQVAE, a generative framework designed to improve the representation of these characteristics in a vector-quantized latent space. We introduce a Large Selective Kernel mechanism to adaptively capture temporal patterns at different scales by dynamically adjusting the effective receptive field. Furthermore, an Efficient Multi-Scale Attention module is integrated to enhance cross-dimensional feature interaction and facilitate the empirical learning of dependencies among process variables. Evaluation on the IndPenSim benchmark shows that Bio-VQVAE achieves the lowest mean values across all four quantitative metrics among the evaluated baseline models. Notably, the method achieves superior fidelity in preserving multivariate correlation structures and temporal autocorrelation consistency, even under constrained data regimes. These results demonstrate the potential of Bio-VQVAE for in-distribution augmentation of multivariate bioprocess time series and for supporting downstream predictive modeling.

title: Grow2Fold: mapping heterogeneous developmental growth to human brain folding
abstract: Cortical folding emerges through complex developmental processes, yet what organizes these processes into the characteristic folding patterns of the human brain remains unclear. Here, we developed an imaging-informed whole-brain modeling framework, Grow2Fold, that integrates developmental cortical regionalization, quantitative growth characterization, and mechanics-guided simulation to investigate how cortical growth shapes brain folding patterns. Using 836 fetal and neonatal MRI sessions from 747 participants spanning 21-45 postmenstrual weeks, we identified a reproducible and hierarchical spatiotemporal organization of cortical expansion characterized by coordinated regional growth trajectories. Rapid expansion occurs earlier around peri-central territories and progressively shifts toward frontal, parietal, and temporal association cortices. We encoded these imaging-derived trajectories into region- and age-specific growth laws and incorporated them into anatomically realistic whole-brain mechanical models. The resulting simulations recapitulate major sulcal landmarks and characteristic folding development across global and regional morphological measures. Comparing regional and uniform growth, we find that differential growth drives cortical instability, while heterogeneous developmental growth organizes this instability into anatomically recognizable folding patterns. Combined with subject-specific anatomy, these population-informed growth laws reproduce individualized longitudinal folding trajectories. Together, our results identify spatiotemporally patterned developmental growth as a key spatial constraint on cortical morphogenesis and establish a quantitative bridge from developmental imaging, through mechanical instability, to anatomically organized folding.

title: Near-null magnetic fields modulate photosystem II function and electron transport in Arabidopsis thaliana
abstract: The geomagnetic field (GMF) has shaped terrestrial life for over 4.2 billion years, yet the mechanisms underlying plant magnetic sensitivity remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the immediate photosynthetic responses of Arabidopsis thaliana to rapid transitions between geomagnetic (GMF; ~45 µT), near-null magnetic field (NNMF; ~30 nT) and hypermagnetic field (HMF; ~1 mT) conditions. Using chlorophyll fluorescence analyses (OJIP and PAM), photosynthetic mutants (ch1, npq1, npq4, and pgr5), Fe-S-cluster-associated lines (KO-isca3, OE-isca3, and atx1), pharmacological (DCMU and NH2OH) perturbation of Photosystem II (PSII), and a simplified quantum spin-Hamiltonian framework, we examined how magnetic-field transitions influence photosynthetic performance. A 10-s transition to NNMF induced rapid increases in fluorescence amplitudes, reduced photochemical operating efficiency, and enhanced photoprotective energy dissipation under actinic illumination. The magnitude and expression of these responses varied among genetic backgrounds and were strongly influenced by donor- and acceptor-side perturbation of PSII. In contrast, HMF produced comparatively modest effects. Together, the genetic and pharmacological analyses indicate that the expression of the magnetic-field-dependent phenotype depends on the physiological state of the photosynthetic apparatus and associated regulatory pathways. Although the molecular origin of the response remains unresolved, the results support further investigation of PSII-associated photochemical and regulatory processes as possible contributors to the observed phenotype. More broadly, this study provides evidence that photosynthetic performance can respond rapidly to magnetic-field transitions and establishes an experimental framework for investigating the processes underlying magnetic-field-associated physiological responses in plants.

title: Polarization of the Drosophila oocyte by active cortical exchange
abstract: Anterior-posterior polarization in the Drosophila oocyte requires posterior localization of oskar mRNA. oskar mRNA is produced in the anteriorly situated nurse cells, moved into the oocyte, and assembled into oskar-Staufen ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs). These RNPs then move through the oocyte and interact with the cortex, where myosin-V binds them to the actin network and kinesin-1 removes them along cortically anchored microtubules. This cortical tug-of-war takes place against an anterior-to-posterior decrease in microtubule density. How the interplay between cytoplasmic transport and cortical binding and unbinding produces a stable posterior cap is unclear. Here, we combine quantitative microscopy, photoconversion experiments, experimental perturbations, and biophysical modeling to show that posterior localization emerges from position-dependent cortical exchange coupled to cytoplasmic diffusion. Our model, which accounts for the tendency of RNPs to demix, suggests that two key parameters that determine the observed localization pattern are the total amount of oskar and the ratio of cortical unbinding to binding rates (the exchange equilibrium constant). Given oskar volume fractions in wild-type, the measured exchange constant is such that oskar localizes to the posterior cortex without demixing. If the balance is broken, say by increasing unbinding rates, oskar irreversibly demixes into cytoplasmic droplets. This is consistent with observations from our experimental perturbations. Our results show how bulk diffusion and cortical exchange, in the face of oskar RNPs' self-attraction, convert a cytoskeletal asymmetry into robust developmental polarity.

title: Ceramic Materials: From Atomic Bonding and Processing to Microstructure, Functional Properties, and Biomedical Applications
abstract: Ceramic materials are inorganic, predominantly nonmetallic solids whose performance is governed by the interplay among atomic bonding, crystal structure, processing, microstructure, and functional properties. Their ionic and covalent bonding provides high hardness, thermal and chemical stability, wear resistance, and diverse electrical behavior, but also limits plastic deformation and increases sensitivity to flaws, porosity, grain boundaries, and residual stresses. This review examines ceramics through the processing--microstructure--property--performance relationship, emphasizing the effects of crystal chemistry, defects, grain size, porosity, and phase stability on mechanical, thermal, electrical, and biological behavior. Conventional sintering, sol--gel processing, and additive manufacturing are discussed as key routes for controlling densification, porosity, geometry, and composition. Biomedical ceramics, including alumina, zirconia, calcium phosphates, hydroxyapatite, tricalcium phosphate, and bioactive glasses, are also reviewed. Emerging topics include nanoceramics, smart ceramics, composites, multimaterial manufacturing, defect engineering, immunomodulatory bioceramics, and sustainable processing. Major challenges remain in brittle fracture, processing heterogeneity, degradation control, scale-up, and the porosity--strength trade-off. Future advances will require integrating advanced manufacturing, multiscale characterization, predictive modeling, and data-driven design.

title: Beyond Dry Flocking: Shape-Dependent Hydrodynamic Alignment
abstract: Flocking results from dynamical alignment among neighbors in a collection of active self-propelling objects. The intervening medium, typically a fluid, however, is not considered to be important for alignment, except for acting as a momentum sink. The flocking system is therefore described as momentum nonconserving "dry" active matter. Here we investigate a confined system of self-propelled Marangoni swimmers where feedback from the fluid medium, which crucially depends on the shape of the swimmers, influences their alignment. Using up to thirty partially camphor-coated triangular paper boats as polar swimmers, we uncover a disorder-to-order transition, and an unusual re-entrant order-to-disorder transition, as functions of camphor concentration and swimmer density, respectively. We reproduce these transitions by formulating a reaction-diffusion model for the camphor field, coupled to the swimmer dynamics, where propulsion forces arise from surface tension gradients. The shape-dependent hydrodynamic interaction discussed here could be central to efficient flocking in living organisms too.

title: Phase-controlled lateral forcing of droplets on a vibrating bath
abstract: We introduce a method for controlling the lateral motion of droplets bouncing on a vibrated liquid bath by superimposing a small periodic rocking motion onto the conventional vertical forcing. We show experimentally that the lateral velocity varies linearly with the rocking amplitude $α$ and sinusoidally with its phase $φ$ relative to the vertical forcing, while the response depends strongly on the droplet's vertical bouncing mode. A time-averaged model of a harmonic bouncer yields a time-averaged lateral force $\overline{F}_x=mgα\sin(Φ_b+φ)$, where $Φ_b$ is the droplet impact phase. Periodic rocking thus provides a simple, programmable means of exerting lateral forces on bouncing droplets, enabling controlled manipulation of passive and active droplets in pilot-wave hydrodynamics.

abstract: We investigate how cotunneling affects passive-state ordering in a Photosystem II reaction center modelled as a nonequilibrium molecular junction. Cotunneling is introduced through a microscopically constructed doubly reduced acceptor state obtained from relevant quinone-side two-electron configurations, while photoexcitation is allowed into the full excitonic manifold. Passive-state permutations are quantified through ergotropy and energetic capacitance. We find that thermodynamic smoothness in ergotropy and energetic capacitance can conceal microscopic state rearrangements. Cotunneling redistributes the extractable nonequilibrium energy among the quinone acceptor, the donor-pheophytin radical pair, and excitonic states with strong contributions from pigments on the inactive branch. At high Coulomb interaction, cotunneling produces no passive-state reordering. Piecewise-linear relations among ergotropy, energetic capacitance, and mean energy further reveal the population reorderings generated by cotunneling.

Here, we apply a nonlinear modes framework to the model and derive analytic predictions for the asymptotic distributions of activation barriers $p(Δ{U})\!\sim\!(Δ{U})^{1/4}$ and the external force needed for the onset of plasticity $p(f_{\rm c})\sim f_{\rm c}^{2/3}$, for their extreme-value scaling and for $\langleΔ{U}\rangle$ beyond the asymptotic regime. We develop efficient algorithms for sampling minima and saddles of the model's glassy potential energy landscape, and quantitatively confirm the theoretical predictions. This progress is enabled by identifying a subset of collective degrees of freedom that are physically relevant for activated glassy dynamics, which like the theoretical predictions should apply to realistic glasses.

abstract: Membrane composition plays a central role in determining how antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) interact with and alter the physical properties of lipid membranes. Here, we investigate the composition-dependent mechanical and structural response of lipid membranes to the AMP aurein using neutron spin-echo (NSE) spectroscopy, neutron membrane diffraction (NMD), and pressure (P)-area (A) isotherms, complemented by previously reported quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS) measurements. In a zwitterionic DMPC membrane, aurein induces progressive softening, manifested by a concentration-dependent decrease in both the bending rigidity and area compressibility modulus. NMD reveals a slight bilayer thinning but no prominent peptide-associated contribution within the deuterated hydrocarbon region, indicating that the progressive mechanical softening is not accompanied by increasingly deep peptide penetration into the hydrophobic core. In contrast, anionic phosphatidylglycerol (PG)-containing DMPC/DMPG membranes exhibit a non-monotonic response, with initial softening followed by pronounced stiffening at higher peptide concentrations. Complementary P-A isotherm measurements independently reproduce these contrasting mechanical responses, showing progressive softening of DMPC but stiffening of DMPC/DMPG. Most importantly, the combined NSE and QENS results reveal a striking multiscale decoupling: aurein suppresses molecular-scale lipid lateral diffusion while simultaneously reducing collective membrane stiffness at the mesoscopic scale, demonstrating that molecular lipid dynamics and collective membrane mechanics can evolve in opposite directions under the same peptide perturbation.Together, these results show that membrane composition governs the collective mechanical response to aurein, while molecular lipid dynamics can respond independently at shorter length and time scales.

abstract: Epithelial tissues undergo dynamic transitions between fluid-like collective motion and mechanically jammed states during development, injury repair, and disease progression. However, the cellular programs that drive these transitions and regulate collective behavior remain unclear. Using a controlled crowding model integrated with live-cell imaging and time-resolved multiomics, we demonstrate that epithelial crowding triggers early metabolic changes characterized by increased mitochondrial pyruvate anaplerosis that precedes the jamming transition. This unjammed state is driven by enhanced cytoskeletal remodeling and requires RhoA-myosin II activity. Mechanistically, we show that elevated cytoskeletal signaling promotes macropinocytic uptake, which serves as a required feedback loop to maintain motility. These findings identify mitochondrial pyruvate utilization as an important regulatory input linking metabolic remodeling to the endocytic control of epithelial fluidity.

title: Kinetic Reduction and Hydrodynamics under Time-Dependent Helical Symmetry
abstract: Translational and helical symmetries provide idealized descriptions of many flows encountered in nature and engineering. While translationally symmetric flows have been extensively studied within kinetic and continuum frameworks, the corresponding connection between microscopic dynamics and continuum behaviour for helical flows is less developed. Here, we investigate this connection for a dilute gas with time-dependent helical symmetry. Using the objective molecular dynamics framework, we derive a reduced Boltzmann equation that retains radial variations while preserving the classical collision operator under helical symmetry. Formal hydrodynamic expansions then yield the corresponding Euler and Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations. The resulting models describe how cylindrical geometry and axial deformation influence transport, including viscous transport and heat conduction, and how deformation generates unequal stresses along and across the axis in competition with collisional relaxation. Comparisons with direct simulation Monte Carlo solutions examine both spatially uniform and radially varying flows. In the cases studied, the first-order fluid corrections capture the leading stress anisotropy and improve the prediction of radial temperature variations, while larger Knudsen numbers expose limitations of the approximation.

Here, we introduce a comprehensive method combining iterative 3D classification, error-rate quantification via simulated particles, and global thermodynamic modeling to extract interaction energies from cryo-EM data. Using hexameric cruciferin (the primary rapeseed storage protein) as a model, we reconstruct a 1.83 [A] structure and distinguish three highly similar 50 kDa isoforms. We resolve the complex compositional heterogeneity of the hexameric species at the single-particle level and fit a global binding model revealing pairwise interaction energies between isoforms differing by fractions of the thermal energy (kB T ). This method offers a powerful, broadly applicable tool to characterize the compositional heterogeneity and energetics of biomolecular complexes.

abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) plays an increasingly important role in structure-based drug discovery (SBDD) by revealing target protein-ligand interactions at the molecular level, but its application has largely focused on large- and medium-sized protein complexes. Many therapeutically important targets are smaller than 50 kDa and remain highly challenging for cryo-EM analysis because of low signal-to-noise ratios and difficulties in particle alignment. Here, we describe cryoFAST, an integrated workflow that couples ligand-compatible Fab discovery and structure-guided computational maturation with biochemical triage, fiducial-complex assembly, and single-particle cryo-EM. Through phage-display screening and/or AI-guided design, we developed high-affinity Fab binders of approximately 50 kDa that stabilize the target without disrupting ligand-target interactions and then assembled Fab-target complexes for cryo-EM analysis. Using the therapeutically relevant extracellular domain (~20 kDa) of interleukin-4 receptor  (IL-4R) as a proof of concept, we determined its cryo-EM structure at 2.74 Angstrom resolution and established a framework for elucidating ligand-binding modes. This workflow provides a practical, efficient, and potentially broadly applicable route to the structural characterization of small protein targets that are otherwise challenging to study. By extending the applicability of cryo-EM to high-value but technically challenging small targets, cryoFAST may open new opportunities for structure-based drug discovery.

title: SCKAnalyzer: A Web Tool for Single-Cycle Kinetics Analysis and Simulation
abstract: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and biolayer interferometry (BLI) are well-established label-free analytical technologies used to determine biomolecular interaction rates (ka, kd) and equilibrium constants (KD). While assays historically rely on multi-cycle kinetics (MCK), this approach requires intermediate surface regeneration, risking sensor degradation and increasing reagent consumption. Single-cycle kinetics (SCK) avoids regeneration by sequentially injecting increasing analyte concentrations. However, implementing SCK workflows on biosensor platforms like the OctetRR8 BLI instrument (Sartorius) remains a challenge due to the lack of built-in or online data analysis tools. To address this, we introduce SCKAnalyzer, a free, user-friendly web application designed for processing and fitting SCK datasets. SCKAnalyzer accepts column-based text files and native raw BLI data (.frd format) from Sartorius instruments, performing data pre-processing and non-linear fitting to a 1:1 interaction model. Additionally, it offers advanced simulation capabilities that allow variable association and dissociation durations across sequential injection steps, a feature absent in existing platforms such as BiacoreTMSimul8. The performance of SCKAnalyzer was experimentally validated using a 3-step SCK method (SCK3) for DNA/RNA duplex formation on a Biacore T200, as well as 4-step (SCK4) and 5-step (SCK5) methods for DNA/DNA duplex formation on an OctetRR8 BLI instrument. Binding parameters (ka, kd, KD) derived from SCKAnalyzer showed excellent agreement with values from established proprietary softwares such as Biacore T200 Evaluation Software v3.2.1 and BIAevaluation v4.1.1. SCKAnalyzer provides a practical alternative to MCK, reducing probe consumption and extending SCK utility across biosensor platforms. SCKAnalyzer is available at sck.iecb.u-bordeaux.fr (source code: github.com/synthaze/sckanalyzer).

abstract: Biflagellate zoospores are critical agents in the spread of Phytophthora spp., plant pathogens causing major agronomic and economic losses worldwide. These motile cells navigate soil water films toward plant roots using taxis triggered by environmental cues. Here, we investigate how potassium modulates zoospore motility by analyzing trajectory and flagellar beating parameters across KCl concentrations. Using high-speed imaging, we apply kymograph analysis and Fourier transform of the cell body direction over time to quantify flagellar dynamics, while low-speed imaging provides trajectory characteristics. Our results demonstrate that increasing potassium concentration significantly reduces swimming speed while enhancing directional changes. We establish a direct correlation between altered swimming speed and changes in flagellar beating parameters. Our findings indicate that potassium differentially affects anterior and posterior flagella beating. Furthermore, potassium exerts multiple effects, influencing beat amplitude, wave propagation speed and direction- change frequency. This reveals potassium as a key modulator of zoospore motility, triggering a shift from exploratory swimming to confined, reoriented movement. By uncovering the biomechanical responses of zoospores to potassium, this study advances our understanding of how surrounding signals regulate pathogen dispersal in the environment.

title: Physical Basis Of pKa Shift For Ionizable Lipids In An LNP-like Environment
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading drug delivery platform for mRNA or other nucleic acid-based therapeutics. LNP platforms are typically composed of ionizable aminolipids, phospholipids, sterols, and lipids tagged with polyethylene glycol. The ionizable aminolipids are typically cationic at low pH, allowing them to encapsulate negatively charged mRNA. The pH at which the ionizable head groups change charge states, the apparent pKa, is crucial to understand the characteristics and formulation of LNP. However, this is difficult to measure as the apparent pKa differs from the pKa of the aminolipids in bulk solution due to the complex chemical and charge environment. In this study, we use molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with alchemical free energy perturbation to calculate the pKa shift as a function of lipid composition, treating LNP-like and vesicle-like environments. Our results show that the pH-dependent structure of the systems affects the trends in pKa shifts in complex ways, driven by factors including surface electrostatics and lipid internalization. Our all-atom simulation protocol allows us to efficiently estimate the apparent pKa of LNP-like models formed with novel ionizable aminolipids and estimate how it will change with composition.
